The city and its housing stock

No county sits between you and city hall here: Virginia Beach is an independent city, and the same government that runs the schools and police bills your property tax. The Atlantic is on its east side and the Chesapeake Bay's mouth on the north, in Virginia's southeastern corner. Of 497.5 total square miles, 244.72 are land and 252.78 are water, and average elevation is about 12 feet. Much of the runoff reaches the Bay by way of the Lynnhaven River and its feeder streams.

A boundary known as the Green Line divides the built-up north from the farmland to the south. Little open ground remains north of it, so resales of older houses in settled subdivisions dominate. The 2020 census counted 459,470 residents and 190,059 housing units, with 6.2% vacant.

A 1963 referendum, approved by voters in both places, merged the city with Princess Anne County. The result has seven boroughs: Bayside, Blackwater, Kempsville, Lynnhaven, Princess Anne, Pungo and Virginia Beach. Neighborhoods such as Alanton, Cape Henry, Great Neck Point, Green Run, Kempsville, Lynnhaven, Pungo and Sandbridge differ in house age and condition.

Which office does what

Value comes from the Real Estate Assessor. Billing and collecting belong to the City Treasurer. The exemption and freeze programs now sit with a third office, the Commissioner of the Revenue. Deeds, wills and plats filed at the Circuit Court clerk's office keep ownership records current.

The tax year is the fiscal year, July 1 to June 30, and payment comes after the fact. Lenders holding escrow get the bill directly, while owners without escrow receive it by mail from the Treasurer. If you pay off the loan or switch lenders, say so, so the bill finds the right recipient.

  • Questions about value or an appeal: 757-385-4601, ask for an appraiser.
  • Board of Equalization: 757-385-6296 or BOE@vbgov.com.
  • Bankruptcy notation on a tax account: email VBBK4you@vbgov.com with the case number.
  • Exemptions and freezes: the Commissioner of the Revenue.

The Treasurer's real estate page also has a tax lookup and an open data portal for delinquent real estate.

Due dates and penalties

Two installments make up the year, December 5 and June 5, and a date on a weekend or city holiday slides to the next business day. Can't cover a bill in full? Partial and advance payments are taken.

Once the grace period ends, a late payment adds a penalty of 10% of the tax or $10, whichever is more, capped at the bill plus interest. Interest accrues at 9.6% a year. Waiting on a reduction does not remove the penalty.

Any payment the Treasurer receives is credited first to the most delinquent account, as Virginia Code 58.1-3913 directs. If a refund is due after a reduction, the city first checks for other delinquent charges, and the refund takes about four weeks.

Years of unpaid tax

Collection can escalate to advertising and a lawsuit. After taxes are three years behind plus the current tax year, the Treasurer may publish the property and its record owner in a newspaper or online and bills a $25 advertising fee.

Still unpaid on June 30 of the fiscal year? The account can go to a law firm, with attorney fees on top. The city may then record a lien at the Virginia Beach Circuit Court and pursue any lawful means, up to a sale of the property.

What happens at a sale when tax is still owed?

Closing pays the overdue tax out of your proceeds. State law ranks the tax lien first among all claims on the real estate, and Code 58.1-3340 keeps it attached until the taxing authority has been paid. A purchaser or trustee completing the sale is responsible for directing the funds to the taxes and levies.

The statute counts penalties and interest as part of the tax. How the year is split between buyer and seller follows the contract, so read both the purchase agreement and the closing statement. The Treasurer prorates by the day from the full annual amount, and the two installment dates do not create separate tax periods. After payment, an officer releases the lien.

The deed carries its own tax. Under Code 58.1-802 the grantor tax is 50 cents per $500 of consideration. Sellers pay it unless the parties agree the buyer takes part. A clerk will not record the deed without certifying that it was paid.

How to challenge your assessment

A phone call to the Assessor is the right opening move, since many concerns get settled that way without added time or cost. If you are still unsatisfied, the written steps are below.

StepWindow
Reassessment notices mailedBy March 1 each year
Request for Reappraisal (informal review)March through April 30 of each tax year
Board of Equalization appealMarch through June 30 of each tax year

An agent may speak for you on valuation only with an original signed letter of authorization or a notarized power of attorney. Six members, appointed by the Circuit Court, sit on the Board of Equalization, and each owns an interest in real property.

Preparing to sell

A little groundwork heads off delays. Look up your parcel through the Treasurer's tax search and confirm that the owner of record matches the deed. If a mortgage company has been paying through escrow, find out when the last payment was made so you know what is still open. If a bankruptcy affects the account, send the case number to the email address above so the notation is correct before closing.

Flooding and weather

Water is the chief physical risk to a house in this city. Humid subtropical weather brings 47 inches of rain a year at the airport and more than 50 at Back Bay, with August the wettest month at over 5.5 inches.

More than 2,000 homes took on water during Hurricane Matthew, and some blocks stayed submerged for days. Afterward the city refused several floodplain building proposals. Shoppers for older houses in low areas ask about earlier flooding and drainage, so keep your elevation certificates, repair receipts and insurance claims handy.

Selling for cash with tax owed

Being behind on tax need not stop you from selling. Get a payoff number from the Treasurer, add your mortgage payoff if any, and measure the total against a cash offer. The tax, penalty and interest are settled from the proceeds at closing, and what remains is yours. Heirs and owners of water-damaged homes are among those who pick this route to skip repairs and a drawn-out listing.

Keep a short file: newest tax bill, mortgage statement, any flood records, and proof of who may sign. With those, a buyer can commit to a firm number and title work can start immediately.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Virginia Beach real estate tax bill due in December?

That turns on your assessment and the current rate, so check your bill on the City Treasurer's website. Installments fall on December 5 and June 5.

What is the penalty for paying Virginia Beach real estate tax late?

Ten percent of the tax or $10, whichever is greater, up to the bill plus interest. Interest is 9.6% a year, and an unresolved reduction request does not waive the penalty.

Can I sell my Virginia Beach house if the property tax is delinquent?

Yes. Under Code 58.1-3340 the tax lien outranks the others, so closing pays the tax, penalty and interest from your proceeds. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure beforehand.

When can I appeal my Virginia Beach assessment?

Ask the Assessor for a reappraisal from March through April 30, or file with the Board of Equalization anytime from March through June 30 of the tax year. Start with a call to an appraiser at 757-385-4601.

Does the Virginia Beach Treasurer or the Assessor decide my value?

The Real Estate Assessor. The Treasurer only bills and collects, so take value questions to the Assessor and payment questions to the Treasurer.

Alexandria at a glance

Alexandria is an independent city on the west bank of the Potomac River, about 15.35 square miles, with Washington, D.C. to the northeast, Arlington County to the north and northwest, and Fairfax County to the south. Because it is independent, it bills its own real estate tax and has no county government above it. The 2020 census counted 159,467 residents, the 2025 estimate is 160,662, and median household income was $124,593 in the 2024 American Community Survey estimate.

The housing mix varies by neighborhood:

  • Old Town, the historic core near the river.
  • Del Ray and Potomac, the former town of Potomac.
  • Carlyle and Eisenhower East.
  • Rosemont, West End, Potomac Yard and Arlandria.

Old Town's historic district, created in 1946, was the third in the country, which is why many Alexandria houses are regulated by a review board.

Transit and commuting

The federal government is the largest force in the local economy, so many buyers work in or near Washington. Metro's Blue and Yellow lines serve the city, with stations at King Street-Old Town, Braddock Road, Eisenhower Avenue and Van Dorn Street, and a Potomac Yard station opened in 2023. The city runs its own DASH bus system, and Interstates 95, 495 and 395 and US 1 pass through it. A house near a station is easy to describe to a commuter, so say so in any listing or call.

Historic district rules

Exterior work in a local historic district needs approval from the Board of Architectural Review. The city regulates two local districts, Old and Historic Alexandria and Parker-Gray, plus buildings designated as One Hundred-Year-Old Buildings.

  • A Certificate of Appropriateness is required for new construction and for exterior alterations visible from a public right of way.
  • A Permit to Demolish is needed to demolish or encapsulate more than 25 square feet of material, whether or not it is visible.
  • Interior work does not need board approval.
  • Staff can approve some projects administratively, usually in under five business days.

The city has a Historic Preservation map viewer for checking whether an address sits in a district. Preservation staff can be reached at 703.746.3833 or Preservation@alexandriava.gov. If you changed the outside of your house, make sure the approval paperwork exists before you list.

What the 2026 assessment showed

Alexandria's total tax base rose 3.41 percent for 2026, the fifteenth straight year of net increase, and residential assessments rose 4.40 percent overall. Of residential properties, 63 percent went up, 8 percent went down and 29 percent stayed the same. Only sales completed before January 1, 2026 counted toward the assessed values.

Tax dates in order

The assessment notice is not a bill. The yearly calendar runs in this order:

  • Late February: assessment notices are mailed.
  • Mid-March: deadline to request an administrative review. The city says no exceptions are made to appeal deadlines.
  • April 15: deadline for elderly and disabled tax relief applications.
  • Late April: City Council sets the tax rate with the budget.
  • June 1: deadline to appeal to the Board of Equalization.
  • June 15: first-half payment due, even if a review or appeal is pending.
  • Early October: second-half bills are mailed.
  • Mid-November: second-half payment due. When November 15 falls on a weekend, the due date moves to the next business day.

To start a review, email realestate@alexandriava.gov or call 703.746.4168.

Tax relief for older or disabled owners

Alexandria runs a real estate tax relief and deferral program for owners who are 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled. Completed applications or annual certifications are due to the Department of Finance by April 15 each year.

  • Household net assets may not exceed $430,000, excluding the home, up to one acre of land and the related mortgage.
  • Household gross income counts the applicant, a spouse and other owners living in the home.
  • Late applications may be accepted until April 15 of the next year for good cause, such as a hospitalization or first-time filing.
  • Deferred taxes are repaid with interest when the property is conveyed or the owner dies. Relieved taxes are not repaid.

The city's phone line is 703.746.4800, option 6, and the email is taxrelief@alexandriava.gov. If you deferred tax, repayment falls due when the house is conveyed, so ask for the balance at the start of the sale.

Flooding near the Potomac

Parts of Old Town flood in storm surge, and some low inlets flood from the tide alone. A city analysis of Potomac gauge data from 2004 to 2021 found the river above Action Stage about 112 days a year and above Flood Stage about 16 days a year.

Hurricane Isabel in September 2003 set the record at 8.66 feet. The Great Potomac Flood of March 1936 reached 7.40 feet, the October 2021 nor'easter 5.99 feet, and Tropical Storm Ernesto in September 2006 5.54 feet. In 2021 the water reached King Street at Strand and Union, and Union Street from Prince to Thompsons Alley. Anyone selling near the waterfront should expect buyers to ask about flood insurance and any past water in the basement or garage.

Deed transfer costs

Virginia's state recordation tax on a deed is 25 cents per $100 under Va. Code 58.1-801, applied to the greater of the price or the most recent assessment. The grantor's tax is a separate 50 cents per $500 under 58.1-802, and it excludes the value of liens that stay on the property. The title company prepares a settlement statement showing these charges and the property tax payoff. Ask it about local recording charges.

Selling with Alexandria tax due

A seller with unpaid tax can still sell, and the title company pays the balance from proceeds. Ask the Treasury Division for a payoff that includes any penalty, and confirm whether the half-year bill already issued has been paid.

Because the first half is due even while a review or appeal is pending, a seller who is contesting a value should still pay on time and keep the receipt. The city offices and a Virginia attorney can confirm figures for your parcel. The first half is due June 15 and the second half in mid-November, moving to the next business day when November 15 falls on a weekend. The city says the first payment is due even if a review or appeal is pending.

How do I appeal my Alexandria assessment?

Request an administrative review by mid-March, then appeal to the Board of Equalization by June 1 if you still disagree. Email realestate@alexandriava.gov or call 703.746.4168.

Does Alexandria have tax relief for seniors?

Yes. Owners 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, can apply by April 15 each year, with household net assets capped at $430,000 excluding the home and up to one acre. Call 703.746.4800, option 6.

Do I need approval to change the outside of a house in Old Town?

Usually yes, if the house is in a local historic district and the work is visible from a public right of way. The Board of Architectural Review issues a Certificate of Appropriateness, and interior work does not need it.

Who bills and collects

Value and billing live in separate city offices. The Assessor's office puts a number on each property, while the Treasurer sends statements and receives payment. Each year, as it finalizes the budget, City Council fixes the rate and the dates. Before you estimate a payoff, ask either office which rate your parcel carries.

The city's fiscal year starts July 1 and ends June 30. More than 68,000 taxable parcels get a bill each quarter, mailed no later than 30 days ahead of the deadline. The Treasurer also collects nuisance abatement liens that Neighborhood Quality refers over, and those must be paid within 30 days.

Quarterly due dates

Norfolk splits the annual bill into four payments. A sale in the middle of the fiscal year can land right after a deadline, so an installment may be freshly due when you list.

QuarterPeriod coveredDue date
1stJuly 1 to September 30September 30
2ndOctober 1 to December 31December 5
3rdJanuary 1 to March 31March 31
4thApril 1 to June 30June 5

Dates are set annually, so when a deadline is near, trust the bill you received.

How to appeal your assessment

An owner can try a conference with an appraiser first, or go straight to a formal hearing before the Board of Review.

  • Informal appeal: phone 757-823-1343 to schedule a talk, in person or by phone. You can book from the day the April notice lands until May 8, or the next business day when May 8 is a weekend.
  • Formal appeal: the Board of Review wants your filing by the last business day of May, received or postmarked.
  • Packet: one original plus five full sets of copies, with a separate application for each parcel.
  • Representatives: an agent needs an original letter of authorization on the owner's letterhead, dated in the same calendar year and notarized.

At the hearing you have five minutes to argue that your value is higher than the market or unequal to comparable homes. Under Va. Code 58.1-3379 the assessor starts out presumed correct, which puts the proof on you. An appraisal you hand in must have been prepared for appeal purposes.

Water, elevation and buyers

Water shapes Norfolk housing. The Elizabeth River runs into the Chesapeake Bay here, and the city's 96.41 square miles include 43.13 of water and 53.28 of land, at an elevation near 6.9 feet. Its 2020 population was 238,005.

Tidal flooding days rose from about five in 2000 to roughly 10 to 15 by 2020, and Hurricane Isabel pushed a surge into the Midtown Tunnel in 2003. After a 2019 study, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers started a Coastal Storm Risk Management project. Locate any elevation certificate or flood zone letter you own and keep it in your listing folder, because buyers raise flooding early.

Flood zones and selling

A buyer's insurance cost can hinge on flood zone, which is why the city offers a property lookup. The zones follow FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Map, with enforcement written into Article 3.9.7 of the zoning ordinance and the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. Through a site named Forerunner, you can look up an address, see flood data and pull any elevation certificates on file.

  • X: outside the 0.2 percent annual chance of flooding.
  • Shaded X: 0.2 percent annual chance, with depths under 1 foot in a 1 percent event.
  • AE, AH and AO: 1 percent annual chance areas, and AE carries a mapped base flood elevation.
  • VE and LiMWA: coastal areas hit by wave action.

In an AE zone, expect the buyer's lender to ask about coverage. In any zone, the tax lien must be cleared before title passes.

Selling with taxes owed

In Virginia the tax lien outranks every other, which means unpaid tax is deducted from what you receive at closing. Va. Code 58.1-3340 tells the purchaser or foreclosure trustee to direct proceeds to the taxes and levies on the property, penalties and interest too. The treasurer then releases the lien.

Put the current quarter's responsibility in writing, since proration is left to the contract. Va. Code 58.1-802 sets a grantor's tax at 50 cents per $500, owed by the seller by default. The circuit court clerk takes it when the deed is recorded, and the proceeds are divided evenly between the state and the city.

Keep the paperwork from each payment, whether it was made online or at the Treasurer's office. A receipt that shows the quarter and the date helps the title company confirm what is settled, and it settles any disagreement about which installment you already covered. If a bill never reached you, request a copy from the Treasurer instead of waiting for the next one to arrive.

Delinquency can end badly. The Treasurer holds online public auctions of parcels with unpaid real estate tax under Va. Code 58.1-3975, sold as is with a 15 percent buyer's premium. Selling before a parcel gets that far keeps price and timing in your hands.

What to do first

Start with an accurate figure. A payoff statement beats a number copied from an old bill.

  • Check with the Treasurer's office, or log into the eBilling portal, to see which quarters remain open.
  • Reach the Assessor at 757-664-4732 for an explanation of how your value was set.
  • Ring the Department of Human Services at 757-823-1130 to learn whether you qualify for real estate tax relief.
  • Warn the title company about any nuisance abatement lien, as the Treasurer collects those as well.

An as-is cash sale avoids repairs and showings, and the title company pays the tax out of the proceeds. That can suit a Navy family with short notice on orders, where a repair list is not realistic.

Before closing day, line up three things. Have the payoff in writing, with the quarter it covers. Confirm with the title company that any abatement lien is on its list. And decide with the buyer how the current quarter will be split, so the settlement statement matches the contract. If a nuisance abatement lien is on the account, the Treasurer collects it separately and the 30 day window may be running, so ask about it early. Each of these steps takes a single phone call, and doing them in this order keeps a routine sale from stalling at the last minute.

An owner who plans to appeal and sell in the same season should remember the timing. The informal window closes May 8 and the formal filing deadline falls at the end of May, while a contract signed in between can change who benefits from a lower value. Talk to your agent and the title company so the agreement says who keeps any reduction.

Frequently asked questions

When are Norfolk real estate taxes due?

Payments are due September 30, December 5, March 31 and June 5. The Treasurer mails bills at least 30 days ahead.

Who do I call about my Norfolk assessment?

Call the City Assessor at 757-664-4732 about value. To book an informal appeal with an appraiser, call 757-823-1343 once your April notice arrives.

When is the Norfolk Board of Review deadline?

Formal appeals are due by the last business day in May. File one application per parcel with an original and five copies.

Can I sell a Norfolk house if I owe property tax?

Yes. The tax lien comes first, so the balance is paid from your proceeds at closing and the treasurer releases the lien. Ask for a payoff figure first.

Does Norfolk auction properties for unpaid tax?

Yes. The Treasurer holds online public auctions under Va. Code 58.1-3975. Selling earlier lets you set the price and the timing.

  • Treasurer: P.O. Box 975, Newport News, VA 23607, phone 757-926-8731, email treasurer@nnva.gov.
  • Commissioner of the Revenue: 2400 Washington Avenue, phone 757-926-8752.

Bills are normally due December 5 and June 5. If you improve the land, say with an addition, the city may send a supplemental bill. Some bills also carry a stormwater fee. If you pay through online banking, enter the grand total for the account number.

How to appeal your assessment

Disagreements over value go to the Board of Review. Hearings take place between September 1 and November 30, and judges of the Newport News Circuit Court name the members each year. Applications are accepted July 1 through September 1, and the city grants no extensions.

  • Weekend rule: if September 1 lands on a weekend or holiday, the next business day is the deadline.
  • Late filings: anything postmarked or hand delivered after the deadline is rejected.
  • Mailing caution: since December 24, 2025, a USPS postmark shows the date the mail was processed, which can be later than the day you dropped it off. Hand delivery or an early mailing is safer.
  • Questions: the Board's administrative assistant, 757-812-7816.

Residential and commercial appeals use different forms. A procedures document for the 2026 cycle and a letter of authorization for agents are posted on the city's Board of Review page. Before the deadline, ask the Assessor for an informal review of your value. That conversation costs nothing and sometimes settles the question.

What buyers ask about Newport News

Newport News had 186,247 residents in 2020. It lies along the James River's north shore at the point where the river opens into Hampton Roads, and 42 percent of its area is water, at an elevation of 15 feet. Prospective buyers often want to know if a home is near a creek, an inlet or a mapped flood zone. Find that out before they ask.

Voters in Warwick and Newport News chose in 1958 to consolidate under one name, so several neighborhoods sit in what used to be the City of Warwick. Shipbuilding, Fort Eustis and the school system anchor local employment, which keeps demand tied to the military and the shipyard.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid city tax gets first claim on the money from a sale. Under Va. Code 58.1-3340, whoever handles the closing, a buyer or a foreclosure trustee, sends part of the proceeds to the city for taxes and levies plus any penalties and interest. The Treasurer then lifts the lien from the title.

Who owes the current year's share is a contract term, so spell out the split in your agreement. A grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of price also applies under Va. Code 58.1-802, charged to the seller unless the two sides negotiate another arrangement. It is paid at the circuit court clerk's office when the deed is recorded.

The Treasurer keeps a page for real estate auctions of properties with delinquent taxes or liens, with the legal notice and auction flyer. If you see a notice for your own parcel, time is short, and a sale you arrange yourself gives you more control over terms than an auction does.

Relief programs

The Commissioner of the Revenue administers the city's relief programs. They include a real estate tax deferral for the elderly and disabled, an exemption for disabled ex-service members, and deferral and exemption programs for mobile homes. The city also offers a Residential Rehabilitation Property Tax Abatement Program with its own calculator, and the Assessor's site has a VA Deed Alert tool.

Income limits and rules are posted on those pages. For state income and tax relief questions, call 757-926-8653. If no program fits and the house needs more work than you can pay for, a cash sale of the property as is can clear the tax at closing instead.

Steps before you close

Begin by requesting a payoff letter from the Treasurer showing the balance, penalties and interest included. Lay it beside your last two bills to see which installments are settled. Next, read the proration clause in your contract. Then make sure the title company has the correct account number, particularly if the bill includes a stormwater fee. Finally, ask the Treasurer's office when records update after payment, since the lien release depends on it.

An as-is cash sale avoids repair negotiations, open houses and a lender's appraisal. Closing still runs through a title company, so a payoff and a settlement statement are part of it. Read both carefully before signing.

Gather a few items before you call the Treasurer or the Assessor: the account number from your bill, the property address, and the name on the deed. If you are calling on behalf of an owner, ask each office what written authorization it wants. The Board of Review page includes a letter of authorization for agents, and the same form is a useful model for other requests. Keep a note of who you spoke with and what each office promised, because a closing can move fast once a contract is signed.

If you plan to appeal and sell in the same year, do not wait. The appeal window closes September 1, and a pending appeal can leave a buyer unsure what the tax will be. Tell your agent and the title company about it so the contract can say who benefits from any reduction.

What is the Newport News property tax rate?

The rate is $1.18 per $100 of assessed value for 2025-26, the same as 2024-25 and 2023-24. City Council sets it each year, so check with the Assessor or Treasurer.

When are Newport News real estate taxes due?

Bills are normally due December 5 and June 5. Improvements to the land may produce a supplemental bill.

What is the deadline to appeal a Newport News assessment?

Applications to the Board of Review run July 1 through September 1, with no extensions. If September 1 is a weekend or holiday, the next business day is the deadline.

How do I reach the Newport News Treasurer?

Write to P.O. Box 975, Newport News, VA 23607, call 757-926-8731 or email treasurer@nnva.gov. Office hours are Monday through Friday, 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

Can I sell my Newport News house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The tax lien comes first, so the title company pays the balance from your proceeds and the Treasurer releases the lien. Get a written payoff before closing.

Due dates

The first half of the real estate tax is due January 14, and the second half is due June 14. January 1 is the date the value of real estate is established. Reassessment notices go out on or about July 1 each year with a value date of July 1, so read your notice for the exact date it uses.

Two equal installments cover the year, on June 5 and December 5. Miss the date and a 10 percent penalty lands on the bill; unpaid balances also pick up interest at 10 percent a year starting July 1. Paying the entire year with the first installment is allowed.

Trust the due date printed on the bill itself. If a bill has not turned up as a due date nears, phone the Treasurer rather than waiting.

A merger on July 1, 1952 joined the city of Hampton, the town of Phoebus and Elizabeth City County into the single city of today. Hampton traces its first English settlement to 1610 and became an independent city in 1908, so land records here run deep. Fort Monroe at Old Point Comfort was decommissioned as an army base on September 15, 2011, and the surrounding area has changed hands and uses since. If your parcel is near the fort or an old waterfront lot, a survey and a clean title search will save a buyer's attorney a lot of questions.

Hampton's neighborhoods range from Aberdeen Gardens and Farmington to Newmarket, Northampton and Hampton Woods, with Buckroe Beach and Fox Hill on the water. Describe condition honestly. An aging roof or a damp crawl space is something an appraiser may never see from the curb. Suffolk's size and what it means for a seller

No Virginia city has more land than Suffolk, which sits in southeastern Virginia's Hampton Roads area. Of 428.91 square miles, 399.17 are land and 29.74 are water. The size dates to 1974, when the original city merged with the former Nansemond County, the city of Nansemond, and the towns of Holland and Whaleyville, all under Suffolk's name. Residents numbered 94,324 in 2020 and an estimated 104,699 in 2025.

Farmland, a piece of the Great Dismal Swamp, small villages and a suburban north end all lie within the limits, so two Suffolk houses can have little in common. The 2020 census recorded 38,364 housing units, with 7.3 percent unoccupied, and 27.1 percent of residents lived in rural areas.

Name your borough

Politically the city has seven boroughs: Chuckatuck, Cypress, Holy Neck, Nansemond, Sleepy Hole, Suffolk and Whaleyville. Whaleyville, Holy Neck and Chuckatuck lean rural. Nansemond, Suffolk, Sleepy Hole and Cypress lean urban.

Tell buyers which borough the property is in, because that hints at lot size, road type and surroundings. The Driver Historic District and the Suffolk Historic District also exist, so an older house deserves a question to the city about any historic overlay before exterior changes.

Drainage, weather and inspections

Summers are hot and sticky, winters mild to cool. Rain totals 51.82 inches in an average year over about 123.7 days, and snow adds roughly 5.8 inches.

With wet weather on roughly a third of days and swamp-edged land, inspectors look at gutters, crawl spaces, drainage and air conditioning. Cleaning and servicing those before you sell can shorten the repair request list.

The city took over its own road system on July 1, 2006, which means road and ditch questions near your house go to Suffolk and not the state.

Local buses come from Suffolk Transit, which has two links to Hampton Roads Transit. Three freight railroads run through.

North Suffolk and the rural south feel like different places on a commute, so give a drive time from the actual address. A buyer who works near the Beltway cares about the northern edge. One who works on a farm cares about the roads to the south, and the city's road system is where questions about a ditch or a bridge approach go.

Pay or ask questions in person at either Treasurer office: downtown at 442 West Washington Street or in North Suffolk at 2000 Bennetts Creek Park Road. Hours are 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, and the number is 757-514-4275.

With quarterly billing, the day you close almost never lines up with a due date. Call the Assessor at 757-382-6235 for a review, apply to the Board of Equalization, or petition Circuit Court. The routes can be combined.

Kemper Street Station handles both Amtrak and Greyhound, and Lynchburg Regional Airport has American Eagle service to Charlotte, which helps buyers who travel. Say so in your listing notes if your street is close to either.

Students and staff from Liberty University, the University of Lynchburg and Randolph College make up part of the rental and buyer pool near campuses, and hospitals such as Lynchburg General and Virginia Baptist draw medical workers. The city has ten recognized historic districts, four of them in the downtown residential area. Petersburg at a glance

The city lies on the Appomattox River roughly 21 miles south of Richmond and had 33,458 residents in 2020. No county sits over it, so the city itself values property, collects other taxes through the Commissioner of the Revenue and Treasurer, and enforces building rules through its code office. Older housing is common here, so buyers will ask about the age and condition of a house.

What to have ready when you call

City staff can help faster when you give them the address, the account or parcel number from your bill, and the name on the deed. If you are calling for a parent or a relative's estate, ask each office what paperwork it wants before it will discuss the account. When you reach Billing and Collections about a payoff, say the date you expect to close, because the figure changes as penalties and interest are added. If a DMV stop is on file for the owner, mention it so it can be cleared in the same conversation. Write down the name of the person you spoke with and the date.

Steps before you close

Work through these in order. Phone Billing and Collections and request a payoff with late charges. Ask the Treasurer which of the four installments you have paid. If the house has stood empty for a year, learn whether it needs registering and whether a fee is due. Ask the Assessor if a supplemental bill is on its way for recent renovations. Finally, hand the closing agent every figure in writing. If any two offices give you different balances, ask both to put their number in an email so the title company can reconcile them before closing. Keep a copy of each payment confirmation. A lender or buyer may ask for proof that the earlier installments were paid, and a printed confirmation answers that question in seconds.

Frequently asked questions

How often does Petersburg reassess real estate?

Every second year, with January 1 as the value date. Owners with a changed value get a notice on January 28 of that year.

What are Petersburg's real estate tax due dates?

Quarterly, on September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30.

What is the deadline to appeal a Petersburg assessment?

For an office review, March 1 or 30 days from the notice. For the Board of Equalization, April 1 or 60 days from the notice.

Do I have to register a vacant house in Petersburg?

Yes, once a building has stood empty for 12 months or more. The yearly registry fee is $100.

Can I sell a Petersburg house with unpaid taxes?

Yes, the title company pays it from your proceeds. Call Billing and Collections, 804-733-2346, for a payoff first.

Charlottesville and its tax bill

Albemarle County wraps around Charlottesville, a central Virginia city on the Rivanna River. The city also serves as Albemarle's county seat, but each has its own government, and a city address gets its bill from the city alone. The city covers 10.27 square miles and counted 46,553 residents in 2020.

The University of Virginia shapes the local housing market more than anything else. Its main grounds are on the west side of the city, although most of the campus is legally in Albemarle County. Ridge Street, Fifeville, Tenth and Page, and Rose Hill are long-standing neighborhoods, and sellers on older streets near the university often own houses with age-related repair needs. Expect a buyer's inspector to focus on the roof and the furnace.

Due dates, rate and penalties

The bill splits into two equal installments, with the rate chosen by City Council each spring. If a deadline falls on a weekend, you have until Monday.

ChargeAmount or dateNotes
First installmentJune 5Half of the annual tax
Second installmentDecember 5Half of the annual tax
Rate$0.99 per $100 of assessed valueConfirm the current rate with the Treasurer
Late penalty10 percent of the tax dueApplied the day after the deadline
Interest10 percent a yearAccrues monthly

The Treasurer's phone is 434-970-3146, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 2854, Charlottesville, VA 22902.

Penalties and interest keep building under a payment plan. For tax that stays unpaid, the city lists bank account liens, rent liens and wage garnishments, and it can sell a property through the courts once three or more years are owed. If you want a penalty waived, read the Late Payment Penalty Policy first, then write to the Treasurer and attach your documents.

How the assessor values your house

Charlottesville reassesses annually. The City Assessor sets each parcel's value as of January 1, and change of assessment notices go out at the end of January, as city code requires.

The usual method for a house is to compare recent sales of similar homes nearby. Auctions, foreclosures, condemnations and sales between relatives generally do not count as arm's-length sales. That matters if a neighboring sale was one of those.

  • Assessor's office: 102 5th Street NE, Charlottesville, VA 22902, by appointment, phone 434-970-3136.
  • Mail: P.O. Box 911, Charlottesville, VA 22902.
  • Commissioner of the Revenue: 605 E Main Street, Room A-130, phone 434-970-3160.

Looking up your property record

Every parcel has a history file at the Assessor's office covering ownership, deed and plat references and the improvements on the lot. Neighborhood maps, land books and GIS data are posted online, the GIS Viewer opens the real estate records, and a public computer at the office gives the same access.

  • Assessment neighborhood maps and land books on the city's assessor pages.
  • An Income and Expense form for income-producing property.
  • An Assessment Appeal Application, which you can also request by phone.

Walk the house with the record in hand before listing. A wrong square footage, acreage or improvement condition counts as a factual discrepancy and is a valid ground for appeal, and fixing it can lower the bill the next owner inherits. An agent filing for you must include a Letter of Authorization.

How to appeal your assessment

An appeal moves through the assessor, then the Board of Equalization, then Circuit Court. Complaining about a high bill or a big increase will not carry an appeal. The city looks for factual errors in the record, values that are uneven across a neighborhood, or a real disagreement over fair market value.

  1. Call the appraiser at 434-970-3136 and give your name, address or nine digit parcel ID. A lot of questions are settled on this call.
  2. File an Assessment Appeal Application with your reasoning and evidence. The appraiser may inspect the property and will mail a decision, which the city says comes within 30 days.
  3. Request a Board of Equalization review within 30 days of the decision letter. Its members are citizens named by the Circuit Court judge, and they mail a decision within 30 days of the hearing.
  4. Last, you can go to Circuit Court, where proof and court costs fall on you.

Ask the assessor's office for the filing deadline on the first application. Under 58.1-3379, the assessor's number is presumed right until you answer it with evidence.

Selling with unpaid tax

Because the Treasurer's balance carries penalty and interest, it moves every month. Request a payoff for your closing date from 434-970-3146 and let the closing agent double-check the amount.

The Commissioner of the Revenue administers relief for elderly and disabled owners, a homeowner assistance program, and an exemption for disabled service members and surviving spouses. Check with that office on which are open before you rely on one.

The seller normally pays the grantor tax, 50 cents per $500 of value, under 58.1-802. Cash Home Buyers can look at a Charlottesville house that needs work or has back tax and make an offer based on the Treasurer's payoff.

What buyers and lenders will ask about

Buyers in a university town tend to ask pointed questions about tax and house age. Be ready to say which installments are paid, what the annual tax is at the city rate of $0.99 per $100, and whether the record matches the house. Older homes near the university may draw questions about the roof, windows and heating system, so have service records handy.

If the assessment notice at the end of January surprised you, say so to the appraiser early. Many questions end with a phone call, and a correction made before you list is easier than one made while a buyer is waiting.

Who handles what in the city

Three offices touch your bill, and each answers different questions. The Treasurer collects payments and quotes payoffs. The City Assessor sets the value and takes appeals. The Commissioner of the Revenue runs the relief programs. If you start with the wrong one, you will usually be redirected, so match the question to the desk before you call.

Appointments are the norm at the Assessor's office, so schedule a visit rather than dropping in. Mail goes to a separate P.O. box for each office, which means a letter to the Treasurer sent to the Assessor's box can lose days.

Steps before you sell

Ring the Treasurer for a payoff and a list of paid installments. Pull your record and look for mistakes in square footage, acreage and improvements. If you find any, tell the appraiser before listing. Planning an appeal? Collect photos, comparable sales and repair estimates, since the application asks for reasoning and evidence.

Selling for cash avoids showings and loan approval delays. Any open balance, penalty and interest included, still comes out of proceeds at closing, so build your plan on the Treasurer's number.

What are the Charlottesville property tax due dates?

June 5 and December 5, in equal installments. A due date that lands on a weekend moves to the next Monday.

What is the Charlottesville real estate tax rate?

$0.99 per $100 of assessed value, set by City Council. Confirm the current rate with the Treasurer, since council sets it each spring.

How do I dispute my Charlottesville assessment?

Phone the City Assessor at 434-970-3136 and, if needed, file an Assessment Appeal Application. Disagree with the decision? The Board of Equalization takes a request within 30 days, and Circuit Court is the last stop.

What happens if Charlottesville property tax goes unpaid?

The day after the deadline a 10 percent penalty applies, and interest runs at 10 percent a year. The city can collect through liens and wage garnishment, and three or more years of unpaid tax can end in judicial sale.

Can I sell a Charlottesville house with tax still due?

Yes. Closing normally pays the balance out of your proceeds, so ask the Treasurer's Office for a payoff dated to your closing.
